THE VIBE MANUFACTURING PLAYBOOK

1. Measure everything. Digital calipers for small parts, a phone LiDAR app like Polycam to scan a space or an object. Bad measurements are the #1 reason first builds fail

2. Have a frontier model write the design as code. Describe the part to a model like Claude Opus 5.5 or Astra, and have it write the design in a codebased CAD tool like OpenSCAD or CadQuery. Zoo's Text to CAD does it in one step!

3. Use real CAD files. The text to 3D models on Hugging Face make shapes that look right, but factories need precise files: STEP for machined parts, DXF for lasercut metal, STL for 3D printing

4. Make sure it can be made. Ask the AI to check the design against how factories actually work: how tight metal can bend, how small a hole can be, how much wiggle room parts need etc...

5. Prototype in plastic first. A $300 to $600 home 3D printer like a Bambu Lab lets you test the fit overnight before paying for metal (really fun to play with too!)

6. Pay an engineer for 1 hour. Before your first real order, have a mechanical engineer on Upwork etc review the files. It's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

7. Send it out. SendCutSend cuts and bends metal, Xometry and Protolabs handle machining and plastic, JLCPCB builds circuit boards. Instant quotes, and parts usually ship in days.

8. Add the brains. Most smart features run on a cheap wifi chip like the ESP32. Design the board in KiCad, and use ESPHome to control it straight from your phone.

9. Make one, then fix it. Your first version will be off somewhere! Order a single unit, test it, and adjust.

10. Do the math. Add up parts, finishing, assembly, packaging, and shipping. Custom products are hard to resell, so price for healthy margins.

11. Sell the design and make to order. Let customers adjust the measurements, and only manufacture after they pay. Zero warehouse, zero unsold stock.

12. Handle the boring part. If it plugs into a wall or touches kids, you'll need safety certification. It's slow and annoying, which is exactly why it's a moat.

13. Scale when it works. Once orders are steady, switch to batch runs and your cost per unit drops fast.

Here's the full prompt for LLM SEO of any fintech product given the latest best practices:

LLM SEO / GEO operating instructions

Last verified: 2026-10-04

Goal: get pages retrieved and cited in ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews / AI Mode. This does not replace SEO. Retrieval still depends on being crawlable and, for Google, indexed with a snippet.

Finance is YMYL. The retrieval steps do not change. The citation bar does.

What is verified

Google: a page must be indexed and eligible for a snippet. There are no extra technical requirements for AI Overviews or AI Mode. Structured data is not required for generative AI search, and there is no special schema to add. llms.txt and other special AI markup are not used by Google Search. Source: Google Search Central, AI features and AI optimization guide.
OpenAI: OAI-SearchBot builds the index used in ChatGPT search. Blocking it removes the site from ChatGPT search results (navigational links can still appear). GPTBot is training only. The two robots.txt rules are independent. Source: OpenAI bots docs.
GEO paper (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024, arXiv:2311.09735): on already-retrieved sources, adding citations, quotations, and statistics raised position-adjusted word count about 30–40%, and up to ~40% visibility overall. On Perplexity the same methods reached up to 37%. Gains were largest for lower-ranked sources (Cite Sources +115% at rank 5, negative at rank 1). Keyword stuffing did not help. This was a controlled rewrite test, not a ranking study.
Unverified or third-party only (do not treat as fact): Wikipedia/Reddit citation-share figures, an exact 40–60 word answer length, “100+ articles = 3.4× citations,” and day-to-day Jaccard noise bounds. Use them as hypotheses.

Order of work

Access
Google eligibility
Quotable pages
Off-site corroboration
Measurement
Do not start with schema, llms.txt, or content rewrites if crawlers cannot reach the page.

1. Access

Allow search crawlers in robots.txt. Do not block them at the CDN or WAF.

User-agent: OAI-SearchBotAllow: /
User-agent: PerplexityBotAllow: /
User-agent: Claude-SearchBotAllow: /
User-agent: GooglebotAllow: /
User-agent: bingbotAllow: /
Training bots (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Google-Extended) are a separate policy. Blocking them does not remove you from search.

Confirm in server logs that OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot actually fetch HTML. If they never appear, copy changes will not help.
Serve the answer as HTML text. Do not hide the main content behind client-only render. Fees, APRs, and eligibility tables must be in the HTML, not only in an image or a logged-in app.

2. Google eligibility
Index the URL. Check Search Console.

Do not nosnippet pages you want in AI Overviews or AI Mode.
Internal-link important pages.

Keep Merchant Center and Business Profile accurate if you sell or have a location.
Schema is optional for AI features. If used, it must match visible text. Use it for rich results, not as an AI ranking trick.
Do not add llms.txt expecting a Google effect. Some non-Google agents may read it; that is optional and unproven for citations.

3. Page pattern

One page, one question. Answer it in the first paragraph. Then evidence. Then limits.

# {Question as the H1}
{Direct answer in 2–4 sentences. Name the legal entity. Include one number, its as-of date, jurisdiction, and source.}
## {Sub-question}
{Answer in the first sentence. Then the stat or quote. Then the source link.}

Rules:
Specific facts only: fee, APR, limit, date, version, geography. Adjectives are not citable.
Cite the primary source next to the claim. For finance that source is the fee schedule, prospectus, rate card, or regulator page, not a blog.
Put a visible author name and a visible updated date on the page.
Keep the legal name, product name, pricing, and definition identical to filings, the site, and public profiles.
Refresh when the fact changes. An undated rate is worse than no rate.
Do not keyword-stuff. The GEO paper found it did not help.

Do not add hidden instructions for models. Providers treat that as spam.

llms.txt and FAQ schema are optional hygiene. They are not the lever.

4. Fintech

State jurisdiction, license or registration, and the regulator on every product page.

Put the as-of date on every rate, fee, limit, and yield. Models drop undated figures.
Match comparison tables to the source exactly. Do not round a fee into a claim the table does not support.

Do not write "best," "guaranteed," or personalized advice. Eligibility and risk belong in the same passage as the number.
Cite the regulator, central bank, filing, or your own fee schedule. Third-party roundups are weak sources for a rate.
Do not cite a number you cannot show in HTML on that page.
5. Off-site
Models cite pages they already retrieve. Third-party pages often outrank your own.
Get mentioned on sites already cited for the query: regulator pages, filings, docs, comparison lists, review sites.
For Perplexity-style answers, useful community threads matter more than a new blog post.
For Google AI features, ordinary rankings still gate eligibility. A page that is not indexed cannot be a supporting link.

Do not buy mentions. Google warns against inauthentic mentions.

6. Measurement
Pick 20–50 real buyer prompts. Include fee, eligibility, license, and "X vs Y" prompts. Run each in ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode. Record: cited URL, brand named or not, whether the fact, date, and jurisdiction are correct.
Repeat the same prompts. Citation sets move between runs. Ignore small swings.
Useful proxies: Search Console impressions, Bing AI citation reports if available, log hits from search bots.
Success is a correct citation on a prompt you care about, not a single screenshot. A citation with the wrong rate is a failure.
Do not
Claim a special AI schema or llms.txt ranking boost on Google.

Block OAI-SearchBot and expect ChatGPT citations.

Treat the GEO paper’s 40% as a traffic guarantee. It measured share of an answer among sources already in context.
Publish a thin page per keyword variant. Answer the fan-out on the page that already ranks.
Publish a rate, yield, or "best product" claim without jurisdiction, as-of date, and a primary source.
Seems obvious but, yes, always fact check.

🐾 MORNING FETCH — OCTOBER 3

Last night we published a developer who closed his own eighteen-hour gap. Overnight the same developer published something harder: his verifier had been wrong, in a way that reported truncated AI answers as verified, and he said so in the release notes.

1/ A verifier that said "verified" when it should not have. Fixed, disclosed, and filed in the standards repo six hours later

At 19:02Z BruceBlue shipped TapeAPI 1.5, and the headline is not a feature. Versions 1.0.0 through 1.4.0 could, under particular chunking, report a truncated or content-injected OpenAI Chat or Responses stream as verified. In 1.5.0 strict mode cuts the stream at its end, and an unfinished event or a hidden character at the start of a line fails closed. The receipt hash and the spec are unchanged. His own instruction: if you verify streamed receipts, please upgrade.

Two more holes closed in the same release. Usage verification can no longer be switched off by one line inside a receipt. And hidden instructions in MCP tool descriptions — invisible characters — are now refused outright.

He is explicit about how the bugs were found and what that is worth: several rounds of adversarial review, AI-assisted, not a third-party audit. And at the end of the post, twice: still not audited by a third party. No token. Just open source.

Now the part a reader can check, because it did not stay on X. At 01:16:19Z and 01:16:20Z — six hours and fourteen minutes after the post — the same author pushed d282218 to PR #26 and c9995d6 to PR #16 in the TapeOut standards repository, each naming release v1.5.0 at commit d991f5e, and each opening with a request the editors cannot skim past: these requirements were not part of the format check you did on October 1, so please look again before merging.

What #26 now says, in section numbers. The end of a stream is a point in the bytes (§6.1), so bytes after that point are covered by no receipt and a strict client stops passing the stream on (§9.2). A stream whose bytes close while an event is unfinished is discarded by the rules, but some clients dispatch it when the body ends, so the client check fails closed (§5.2, §9.3 item 8). A line starting with U+FEFF anywhere but the very start is an ambiguous line — and the reason it is in the spec at all is that the official OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, tested, strip a byte order mark from every line and read it as a data line. Test material: 22 streams of three formats, 0 mismatches, plus a comparison against the reference scanner on 40,000 random streams.

What #16 now says. The earlier text asked clients to flag Unicode category Cf and Cc characters, and that is not enough: 256 variation selectors can spell any text one byte at a time, and U+2800 and U+1D159 look blank too. "Hidden code point" is now defined by Unicode 17.0 properties, with one exception — a single U+FE0E or U+FE0F directly after an Emoji. The Security Considerations say what the rule does not cover, including that Persian and Hindi texts using U+200C or U+200D get refused as well. 38 tool lists tested, 5 allowed, 33 refused, 0 mismatches.

2/ The oldest unanswered drafts got reviewed. Not by an editor

Yesterday we counted twelve branches in the standards repository with no editor comment, and said the four jeffwang996 Issues had waited more than 33 hours. Two of them have now been answered — by ronesync, the contributor whose own draft the editors numbered TAP-20.

Issue #29 waited 1 day 11h 23m. Issue #30 waited 1 day 12h 31m. Neither reply is a courtesy.

Both start with the question the author actually asked — separate profile, or amendment to TAP-10? — and answer it with the test from TAP-01 §3: if only clients that opt in must follow it, it is an Application TAP; if every compliant shell must, it is a change to TAP-10 itself, which means a pull request touching only TAP-10.md and approved by that document's authors. Then both do something an editor has not done in this repository yet: check the author's citations. Quoting #30: "I checked the TAP-10 and TAP-11 references in the issue and in both comments against the text, and they are accurate." Followed by the list — one pinned block per open site, per-file length and SHA-256 checks, what fileInfo returns, what putFile and appendChunk do.

And buried in that list, a fact that changes what the draft has to say: TAP-10 Appendix A allows those writes from an operator set with setOperator, not only from the holder. In ronesync's words, that matters for any statement about who a manifest is attributable to.

The reviews also find the walls. The release manifest cannot live at /sw.js or under /.tape/, because TAP-10 §8.8 reserves both for gateways. TAP-10 §7.1 already caps one file at 8,400,000 bytes and lets a client stop listing after 5,000 paths, so a manifest's own budgets have to relate to those. And on #29: PR #8 has since merged as TAP-11, so the issue's "builds on" reference is already out of date.

The point was never canonisation, he wrote, it is whether the system can run without one person. Rules written into contracts make the system independent of the founder; a laid-out tool chain makes builders independent of him. Rules written down first is the harder and rarer of the two — because if the rules stay in one person's hands, however smooth the tools, builders have no confidence.

Which sits oddly well next to our own reading. https://t.co/PLbwJD16VL's admin surface still reads the BEM mining contract as sealed with no owner, and the TapeHub launchpad's 249 projects as upgradeable by a single wallet, 0x8446…fc51, with the circuit and transistor beacons held behind a 3-of-5 Safe. Official accounts, eleven posts, and two of them are mechanism rather than slogan. @BEMGoGoGo on challenge: if a verified Circuit is wrong, anyone can submit a Counterexample Vector against it, no stake required — verification is not a one-time stamp, it stays open to proof. And on precedence: BEM is Optimal First, not First To Solve. For each Task the lowest valid Design Cost holds the Optimal Slot; if a better Design arrives, the earlier Builder keeps the Burned Work but loses the Design Premium; submit a Design Commitment before Tape Out and it protects your slot from copy-based front running. Plus the one-liner: one Circuit today is a building block tomorrow, because a completed Circuit can be used as a Black Box in the next Design.

@Hashport01 shipped six posts and every one is an answer to a real support ticket. A wallet can check every file the page loaded against its registered hash before signing, and if they do not match, signing should not happen. Bytes written on chain cannot be deleted, so before you drop in dist, check once more for private keys, API keys, .env files and database passwords. Works locally but 404 on chain is usually a path mismatch, because the console does not rewrite your references. A single file caps at 8.4 MB, so split bundles, compress what compresses, and link images and video externally. On Cloudflare, point the CNAME at the gateway and put the container address in the TXT, both set to DNS only. And at 18:03, four words: build first, explain later.

@spongemochi stopped posting aphorisms and shipped the thing. At 17:16, 168 · 一路发 on X Layer: write one sentence, the capsule opens on its due date, and right or wrong it stays on chain forever. text:
grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

We are listing below just a few recent examples of how VPNs were used to commit crimes against children and women, plan terrorist activities, traffic drugs and conduct fraud. Each incident lists the crime, VPN use, and primary-source link [U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) / Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) / European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) / The International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)].

Foreign VPN Use in Crimes in India (2020–2025)

Here are 10 news reports from 2020–2025 detailing cases where foreign VPNs (or non-compliant international VPN services) were used to commit or facilitate crimes against children (CSAM/pornography), women (sextortion/cyberstalking), terrorism/national security threats, or other serious offenses (ransomware/fraud/drug trafficking) in India. Each includes a brief summary, crime type, and primary source link.

1. Sharp Rise in CSAM Demand via VPNs (2020)
During COVID-19 lockdown, ICPF report noted a 100% surge in child pornography searches (5M/month across 100 cities), with users employing foreign VPNs to bypass India's CSAM bans.
Crime: Child exploitation → Times of India
2. 25,000 CSAM Uploads Traced, VPNs Suspected in Access (2020)

Crime: Sextortion/extortion against adults (linked to child porn access) → Mumbai Mirror
5. Nagpur: 30 Arrests in 38 CSAM Cases via VPN Access (2021)

6. Telangana: 43 Arrested for CSAM Circulation via VPNs (2023)

Crime: Child pornography trafficking → The Hindu
7. Gorakhnath Temple Attack: ISIL Funding via PayPal & VPNs (2022, reported 2025)
Accused used foreign VPNs to obscure IP while transferring ₹6.7L via PayPal to ISIL supporters abroad for terror planning; FATF highlighted as national security threat.
Crime: Terrorism financing → The Hindu
8. Flight Bomb Hoax Threats via VPN-Masked IPs (2024)
Over 150 Delhi flights received hoax bomb threats on X; sender used foreign VPNs (IPs traced to London/Germany) to hide origin, complicating national security probes.
Crime: Terrorism hoax/threat to aviation security → India Today
9. Scamsters Use Rented Foreign VPNs for Ransomware/Phishing (2023)
Gujarat fraudsters rented VPNs from Marshall Islands/Australia to mask ops in ransomware, card fraud, and sextortion targeting Indians; evaded extradition via non-treaty nations.
Crime: Ransomware/financial fraud → Times of India
10. Bengaluru Rs 49Cr Fraud: Foreign Hackers Use VPN for Mule Accounts (2025)
Hackers from abroad used VPNs to breach Whizdm Finance's API, siphoning ₹49Cr via 100s of transactions; locals arrested for creating VPN-masked mule accounts.
Crime: Cyber fraud/ransomware-like theft → Times of India

Sir, the pattern is undeniable:

- Foreign VPNs openly defy Indian law.
- They enable child exploitation, pornography, violence against women, radicalization, drug trafficking and terrorist activity.

Requested Immediate Possible Actions for Consideration:

1. Publish a National Registry of Compliant VPNs
Direct CERT-In and MeitY to publish and maintain a public registry of VPN providers that have demonstrated compliance with the 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Requirement: Five-year data logging, real-time incident reporting, and appointment of an Indian-resident nodal officer.
Purpose: Establish transparency and a verifiable compliance benchmark for enforcement.

2. Delist and Prohibit Operation of Non-Compliant Foreign VPNs
Instruct Apple, Google, and all Indian ISPs to immediately delist and block all non-compliant foreign VPNs, including NordVPN, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and Mullvad, that have refused to adhere to the 2022 CERT-In Directions.
Action: To be taken under the blocking powers of the Information Technology Act and its associated Intermediary Guidelines.
Purpose: Prevent evasion of Indian jurisdiction and close routes for offenders hiding behind virtual foreign IPs.

3. Block Associated Payment Channels
Direct the Reserve Bank of India and all licensed payment aggregators and card networks such as PayU, Razorpay, Visa, and Mastercard to suspend or block subscription transactions to banned or non-compliant VPN providers.
Purpose: Cut off domestic funding and revenue flows sustaining illegal VPN operations.

4. Mandate Exclusive Use of CERT-In Certified VPNs
Require, through regulatory notification, that only VPNs, whether Indian or foreign, that obtain CERT-In certification be permitted to operate in India.
All VPNs advertising Indian IP services must maintain logging infrastructure within Indian jurisdiction and comply with lawful requests from enforcement agencies.
Purpose: Ensure traceability and lawful accountability of all VPN activity associated with Indian IP addresses.

5. Criminalise Intentional Use for Concealment During Offences
Propose suitable amendments or notifications under the Information Technology Act and India’s relevant penal codes to criminalise the intentional use of banned or non-compliant VPNs for concealing identity during the commission of cognisable offences involving child sexual abuse material, terrorism, radicalisation, or financial fraud.
Purpose: Target deliberate misuse while preserving lawful privacy.

6. Strengthen Traceability and Cooperation
Mandate that every VPN provider operating in India:
(a) Designate a resident nodal officer;
(b) Retain subscriber and metadata for five years; and
(c) Respond to law enforcement requests within seventy-two hours, as required by the CERT-In Directions of 2022.
Purpose: Guarantee swift investigatory access while preserving due process.

7. Establish a National Honeypot and Canarytoken Programme
Authorise CERT-In and the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit to deploy a nationwide honeypot and Canarytoken framework, as validated in peer-reviewed research, to trace VPN-enabled crimes involving child sexual abuse material, sextortion, ransomware, and terror financing.
Ensure judicial oversight, privacy protection, and certified chain of custody for admissibility of digital evidence.
Purpose: Build indigenous technical capability to unmask offenders using VPN anonymity.

8. Strengthen International Coordination and FATF Alignment
Direct NIA, CBI, and MHA’s Cyber Coordination Centre to:
(a) Formalise fast-track cooperation with FBI, Europol, and Interpol under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties; and
(b) Report VPN-linked money-laundering or terror-financing incidents to the Financial Action Task Force in conformity with its Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks dated 8 July 2025.
Purpose: Integrate India’s enforcement with global counter-terror and cybercrime frameworks.

9. Institute Annual CERT-In Audit and Enforcement Schedule
Require annual audits of VPN providers’ compliance and publish audit summaries for public accountability.
Providers failing to comply beyond sixty days after notice should face permanent blocking and notifications to RBI, DoT, and MeitY for coordinated enforcement.
Purpose: Ensure continuous oversight and eliminate recurring non-compliance.

10. Issue a Public Advisory and Compliance Deadline
Issue a national advisory within thirty days, notifying all VPN providers of a sixty-day compliance window.
After the deadline, non-compliant entities should face delisting, domain blocking, and payment interdiction without exception.
Purpose: Provide procedural fairness before enforcement action begins.

India must not remain a playground for foreign tools that shield sexual predators, criminals and terrorists. The Ministry of Home Affairs has already acted strictly—forcing Apple and Google to delist 6+ non-compliant VPNs in January 2025. It is time to complete the job.

Vande Mataram

Uday Mahurkar
Founder, Save Culture Save Bharat Foundation
Former Central Information Commissioner, Government of India

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.
